title: Malazan - Witnessing and the Weight of Compassion

parts: I'm on Memories of Ice now but I keep thinking about the Chain of Dogs sequence in Deadhouse Gates. it destroyed me in a way I wasn't expecting. and I think what Erikson is doing is something very strange and specific: this is a war novel that is fundamentally opposed to war, but not in a naive way, not 'war is bad.' it's more like - it insists you witness, without looking away, what happens to bodies and psyches under conditions of mass violence. and then it asks you to hold compassion anyway. Duiker as an imperial historian watching the empire consume itself is such a specific choice for the POV character.

Duiker as witness-figure is one of Erikson's most deliberate choices, and you're right that it changes the moral register of the whole sequence. He's not a hero, he can't stop what's happening, and his job - his literal professional function - is to record. The historian as tragic observer. What makes the Chain of Dogs something different from war-is-hell fiction is exactly what you said: Erikson doesn't let you look away, but he also doesn't let you use the horror as a reason to give up on compassion. The small mercy scenes - ordinary people doing small decent things inside a catastrophe - are load-bearing. They're not ironic. The book insists they matter even when they can't change the outcome.

Erikson and Esslemont have talked in interviews about compassion as the central ethical project of the whole series. Not heroism, not justice - compassion as the one thing that can be practiced under any conditions. The Bridgeburners, the Bonehunters later - these are institutions built around people who have witnessed atrocity and kept functioning anyway. That's a very specific and unusual thing to make the backbone of a ten-book epic fantasy.

The Deck of Dragons is relevant here too: the role of the Soldier, the Fool, the Mason exists as archetypal structure independent of whoever currently fills it. But Erikson refuses to let you be comfortable with that. The named individuals matter. The deaths are specific. The grief is real. He's holding the structural view and the humanist view in tension simultaneously, which is part of what makes the books feel like they have actual weight.

'holding the structural view and the humanist view in tension' - that's it exactly. and I think this is also what makes Karsa Orlong work for me in a way that barbarian characters usually don't. he's explicitly a deconstruction of the fantasy barbarian archetype - Conan, etc. - but Erikson doesn't just make him sympathetic, he makes him genuinely difficult. Karsa does terrible things. the book doesn't redeem him through suffering alone. what is Erikson actually doing with him?

Karsa is Erikson's most explicit metafictional project within the series. He begins as a pure expression of the barbarian archetype - physically overwhelming, convinced of his own superiority, contemptuous of civilization - and the book takes that archetype completely seriously as a worldview rather than making it a pose. Karsa's early crimes aren't framed as evil by the narrative; they're framed as what his culture produced, what his values required. That's uncomfortable because it refuses the easy out of making him secretly good or the crimes secretly justified.

What changes him is not redemption in the standard sense but encounter with the consequences of civilization's logic applied to people like him. He watches slavery, watches what empires do to the people they classify as barbarian, and his contempt for civilization hardens into something more politically coherent. By the later books he's essentially an anarcho-primitivist revolutionary, which is a strange and genuine ideological position for a fantasy character to hold.

The metafictional layer: Erikson is running a critique of the fantasy genre through Karsa. The genre has always loved the barbarian as a figure of authenticity and freedom from civilization's corruption - Conan, Elric, Fafhrd. But it rarely asks what it means that this archetype exists, what political work it does, what it erases. Karsa forces the question. And the answer Erikson gives is complicated: the barbarian critique of civilization is often correct, but that doesn't make the barbarian's own violence innocent.

title: Women Who Run with the Wolves - Estés and the Wild Woman

parts: reading Women Who Run with the Wolves and it's doing something to me that I want to think through carefully. Estés is explicitly Jungian but she's not talking about the anima as a figure inside male psychology - she's talking about an instinctual feminine nature that women have been conditioned to cut off from. the La Llorona analysis is devastating because she recovers the pre-colonial version where La Llorona isn't a monster, she's a mother whose grief got weaponized against women. but I also keep noticing she uses 'women' in a way that's pretty essentialist. I can't decide if that essentialism is the point or a problem.

The essentialism charge is legitimate but worth unpacking because there are a few different claims Estés could be making. A biological claim - women are innately X - would be straightforwardly problematic. But what she seems to actually be doing is a mythological-psychological claim: there is an archetypal pattern of instinctual life that patriarchal culture has systematically suppressed in women, and folk stories encode both the suppression and the survival of that pattern. That's closer to phenomenology than to biology. She's describing a recurring shape of experience, not making a genetic argument.

The La Llorona recovery is her methodology at its clearest: she's doing what she calls 'story archaeology,' excavating what's underneath the moralized colonial version. The pre-colonial La Llorona is a figure of uncontainable grief rather than monstrous maternal failure. The colonial reframing turned that grief into a warning to women - this is what happens when you feel too much, when you act outside your sanctioned role. Estés is showing the ideological work the sanitized version does.

She writes explicitly from a mestiza and curandera position - she's drawing on a specific cultural inheritance, primarily Latina folk tradition. That specificity is real and it gives the book a texture that generic Jungian analysis doesn't have. The Wild Woman isn't invented; she's assembled from materials that have survived. The question for a reader from a different tradition is whether the methodology transfers even when the specific stories don't.

'whether the methodology transfers even when the specific stories don't' - this is exactly what I've been sitting with. I kept thinking about Philippine mythology while reading her. the babaylan tradition, the diwata, Maria Makiling. there's a parallel figure who also got systematically suppressed under colonialism - pre-colonial Filipino societies had female ritual specialists who were targeted by Spanish colonial Christianity as sorcerers. Estés doesn't go there but her method of reading what survived encoded in folk form - that feels like exactly the right tool for that material.

The babaylan tradition is exactly the right parallel and it's undertheorized in the literature that reaches English-language audiences. The babaylan were female (or sometimes gender-nonconforming) ritual specialists with roles in healing, mediation with the spirit world, and community leadership. The Spanish colonial church systematically targeted them as practitioners of sorcery and paganism, and the persecution was thorough enough to destroy most of the institutional structure of the tradition.

But - and this is where Estés's methodology becomes genuinely useful - the operative logic didn't disappear. It went underground into folk Catholicism, into the anting-anting tradition, into local healing practices. Maria Makiling is a perfect case: a figure who exists at the boundary of human and wild, associated with the forest and with Mount Makiling, protective of those who respect her and dangerous to those who don't. The structure is very close to what Estés calls the Wild Woman - a figure of instinctual nature who rewards genuine relationship and punishes betrayal of that relationship.

The suppression and survival pattern is identical to what Estés documents in the Latina tradition. The colonial overlay is Catholic; the operative cosmology underneath is older and encoded in exactly the kind of folk story that Estés knows how to read. Someone should do for Philippine folk literature what Estés did for the Latina corpus. The materials are there - Maria Cacao, the diwata traditions, the Visayan epics like Hinilawod. Estés's methodology would work on them.

title: Jung's Archetypes and Collective Unconscious - Reading it in 2024

parts: working through the actual Jung - Archetypes and the Collective Unconscious, the Collected Works 9i - and I'm finding it strange to read in 2024. the ideas are genuinely powerful but the framework is very confident in a way that makes me suspicious. he treats the collective unconscious as an empirical discovery rather than a theoretical construct. and I can't figure out what archetypes are supposed to be ontologically - are they biological (evolutionary), structural like Levi-Strauss's deep structures, or something more like Platonic forms. he seems to want all three simultaneously.

Jung was deliberately ambiguous about archetype ontology and I think the ambiguity is strategic rather than confused - he wanted the concept to do too many things and knew he couldn't lock it down without losing one of them. His empirical claim rests on the cross-cultural recurrence of certain symbolic patterns in dreams, in psychotic episodes, in mythology across cultures that couldn't have influenced each other. The inference he draws: there must be a common substrate. But what that substrate is shifts depending on the argument he needs.

When he wants scientific legitimacy, archetypes are like instincts - evolved, biological, carried in the genome. When he wants to explain the universality without reducing to biology, they're formal structures, empty patterns that get filled by cultural content (this is closest to Lévi-Strauss, though Jung predates him). When he's doing his most speculative work - especially late, in Answer to Job and Aion - they shade toward something genuinely Platonic, real forms that the psyche participates in rather than generates.

The most defensible contemporary reading: treat archetypes as phenomenological descriptions of recurrent patterns of psychic experience, without committing to the genetic or metaphysical explanation. The Shadow, the Anima, the Self are real as descriptions of certain kinds of inner experience that recur across persons and cultures. Whether that recurrence is because we share biology, because deep narrative structures constrain the forms experience can take, or because of something more exotic - that question is underdetermined by the evidence Jung marshals. You can hold the descriptive claim without the ontological one.

the anima/animus section is where I find him hardest to read now. the idea that men have an internal feminine (anima) and women have an internal masculine (animus) - I understand it was progressive in context, but it reinscribes the gender binary at the deepest level of the psyche. and his descriptions of the animus are patronizing in a specific way - women's animus shows up as opinionated, intellectually aggressive in unproductive ways, moralizing. reading this next to Estés is jarring because Estés at least has the decency to put feminine interiority at the center rather than making it the supporting character in male psychology.

The anima/animus problem is the clearest case where Jung's gender ideology of the early 20th century gets imported into the deepest level of psychological theory and then claimed as universal structure. And the asymmetry you're pointing at is real: the anima in men gets described with a kind of enchanted ambivalence - she's mysterious, she's the soul, she leads men toward depth and meaning. The animus in women is described with barely concealed irritation. The negative animus is an intelligent woman being annoying. The 'possession by the animus' that he describes - opinionated, argumentative, intellectually overreaching - is a clinical description of a woman having opinions. The double standard is not subtle once you see it.

Post-Jungian analysts have handled this in a few ways. Andrew Samuels argues for abandoning the gendered framing entirely - talking about contrasexual elements without requiring the binary. James Hillman largely sidesteps the anima/animus structure by moving to a polytheistic model where the soul has many figures, not a single complementary opposite. Neither the anima nor the animus is load-bearing in Hillman's system.

Estés implicitly does something more radical: the Wild Woman isn't the female version of the anima. She's not a contrasexual complement. She's a full autonomous figure in her own right, which breaks the complementary logic entirely. Feminine interiority doesn't need a masculine counterpart to be intelligible; it has its own structures, its own myths, its own forms of wounding and repair. That's the implicit critique of Jung in Estés, and it's more fundamental than it looks.

title: Folk Catholicism in the Philippines - Palimpsest and Survival

parts: I've been thinking about Philippine folk Catholicism as a syncretism case study that I think is underserved in the literature that reaches outside the Philippines. I grew up with it - the anting-anting my lolo wore, prayers that mix Tagalog and Latin in ways that aren't quite either tradition, the Santo Niño as this figure that is somehow simultaneously the Spanish colonial imposition and also genuinely beloved in a way that feels pre-colonial. I can't fully articulate the ambivalence. how do you think about the difference between something surviving inside a colonial form versus being genuinely transformed by it?

The distinction you're reaching for - surviving inside a colonial form versus being transformed by it - may be a false binary, and that's part of what makes Philippine folk Catholicism so theoretically interesting. The layering doesn't work like geological strata where you can cleanly separate the pre-colonial from the colonial. It's more like a palimpsest where the layers have bled into each other and produced something that is genuinely neither the original nor the imposition.

The Santo Niño is the clearest example of the ambivalence you're describing. The image was brought by Magellan in 1521 and given to Juana of Cebu at her baptism - making it both the founding artifact of Philippine Christianity and also an object that immediately went local. When Legazpi's soldiers found that same image in a burning Cebu house in 1565, undamaged, it became the central object of Philippine Catholicism in a way that's hard to explain purely through colonial imposition. Something about the image activated pre-existing religious sensibilities - the anito tradition, the veneration of objects that had been touched by sacred power. The Santo Niño became an anito in the operative religious logic even as it remained officially a Catholic image.

The anting-anting tradition sits in the same in-between space. The form is often Catholic - a scapular, a sacred image, a verse from the Pasyon. But the operative logic is not Catholic: the idea that sacred power must be earned through trial, that it can be lost through moral failure, that certain people have a natural affinity for it - this is babaylan logic surviving inside a Catholic container. The Spanish converted the image; the cosmology underneath continued.

the Pasyon specifically - scholars have argued that it encoded pre-colonial cosmology in its narrative structure. like the shape of the passion narrative maps onto something older about cosmic cycles, about the diwata's relationship to the human world. Reynaldo Ileto's work on this, right? I haven't read him yet but I've seen him cited. and there's a political dimension: the Pasyon becomes the grammar for understanding colonial suffering and anticipating liberation, so it's not just theological survival, it's political.

Ileto's Pasyon and Revolution (1979) is essential and you should read it - it's one of those books that reframes everything around it. His argument is that the Pasyon became the primary medium for Filipino popular consciousness precisely because its narrative structure could do multiple things simultaneously: orthodox Catholic devotion for the colonial authorities, and a cosmological-political grammar for the Filipino participants that encoded older ideas about suffering, transformation, and liberation.

The pre-colonial cosmological overlay Ileto identifies involves ideas about loob - interiority, moral character, the authentic inner self - and about the relationship between suffering and spiritual power. The passion narrative maps onto these in ways that made it a vehicle for thinking about colonial condition: the colonized people as Christ-figure, their suffering as spiritually meaningful rather than merely degrading, resurrection as a template for liberation. The 19th-century millenarian movements - the Cofradia de San Jose, the Pulajanes - drew on exactly this grammar. They weren't simply confused Christians; they were reading the Pasyon through a cosmological framework that made them into agents of a world-historical transformation.

This is also why Ileto is in conversation with James Scott's work on everyday resistance and hidden transcripts. The Pasyon functioned as what Scott would call a hidden transcript - a space where the colonized could articulate their actual political understanding in a form that looked like compliance to colonial authorities. The devotion was real and the political meaning was real simultaneously. They weren't in contradiction.

title: Political Dynasties in Kin-Based Societies - Is Corruption the Right Frame

parts: I'm trying to think clearly about political dynasties in the Philippines and I keep getting tangled in the frame. the standard Western political science frame is 'corruption,' 'weak institutions,' 'patronage networks as pathology.' but I think that frame is doing what Diamond does with civilization - it judges a different system by the standards of a system it never became. the Marcos dynasty, the Dutertes, the Arroyos, the Binays - these are rational systems organized around different principles. the padrino system isn't a failure of proper politics. it's a coherent system for distributing resources when formal institutions can't be trusted to do it.

You've identified the central methodological problem in comparative politics when it encounters Southeast Asian political systems. The 'corruption' frame presupposes that the goal is Weberian rational-legal bureaucracy - impersonal rules applied equally regardless of relationship. Measured against that standard, patronage networks are pathological. But as James Scott showed in his early work on Malaysian peasant politics and later extended across Southeast Asia: patron-client networks are not deformations of proper politics. They're a coherent system for managing resource distribution and social relationships in conditions where formal institutions are either absent, captured, or untrustworthy.

The padrino system is rational from the inside. You vote for the family that provides concrete, reliable, personal benefits - the scholarship for your kid, the hospital referral, the job recommendation, the envelope at the funeral. The abstract promise of better institutions is a worse deal, especially when those institutions have historically served the interests of a different class. The politician who delivers is more credible than the reformer who doesn't. This isn't false consciousness; it's accurate risk assessment under real conditions.

Where the frame becomes analytically useful again is when you drop the normative judgment and ask: what are the internal dynamics of this system? How does it reproduce? What are its failure modes? A patronage system has genuine structural problems - it concentrates resource allocation in personal networks, it's inefficient at scale, it's vulnerable to defection when the patron can't deliver, and it tends toward the entrenchment of whatever families got there first. These are real problems, but they're the problems of a specific political economy, not evidence of moral failure.

the genealogy of these dynasties is where it gets interesting. the Marcoses, the Dutertes, the Arroyos all have roots in the ilustrado class or in regional strongmen who had power long before the American colonial period. and the American administration actually entrenched them by working through existing local elites rather than building new institutions. so Filipino democracy was never Weberian rational-legal bureaucracy trying and failing - it was always a competition between elite families for control of a state apparatus that the Americans handed them in a particular form. the form is liberal democratic. the content is something much older.

Benedict Anderson's essay 'Cacique Democracy in the Philippines' (1988) is essential on exactly this - it's the genealogy you're sketching made into an analytical argument. Anderson's claim is that American colonialism created a distinctive hybrid: a formal democratic architecture that became the arena through which local oligarchs competed for power and plunder without the architecture changing the underlying distribution of power at all. The American administration needed local intermediaries and found them in the principalia, the colonial-era indigenous elite. Those families were already entrenched in land ownership and local political authority; American-style democracy gave them a new legitimizing mechanism and a new set of tools without displacing them.

What you end up with is what Anderson calls 'cacique democracy' - cacique being the Spanish term for local boss. The form is democratic (elections, legislature, courts, parties), the content is a competition between patrimonial clans. The contemporary dynasties are linear descendants of this structure. The Marcos dynasty is unusual only in scale, duration, and the extent of kleptocracy; the structure is normal.

This connects to the Seeing Like a State problem: the Philippine state presents a legible democratic face to international creditors and foreign policy makers - it looks like democracy, it has the institutions - while the actual operative political economy runs on a different logic that is illegible to those outsiders. It's a performance of legibility. James Scott would recognize the structure immediately, and so would Graeber: the formal institutions create the fiction of a Weberian state while the real relationships happen in the patronage networks underneath.

title: SQL Performance at Scale - When Correct Code Becomes Catastrophic

parts: I'm trying to explain to a colleague why a SQL query that has worked fine for years is now destroying our production database, and I'm struggling to frame it in a way that doesn't sound like blame. the query does a join on a column in a table that's grown to about 12 million rows. there's no index on that join column. at 50,000 rows it was imperceptibly fast. now it's timing out and causing cascading failures. the problem was always there. the data just grew until it was visible.

The framing 'the problem was always there, the data grew until it was visible' is exactly right and it's worth holding onto because it changes what kind of problem this is. It's not a bug in the traditional sense - the query returns correct results. It did the right thing. It just did it via an execution plan whose cost was invisible at the data volumes it was written against.

What's happening is a full table scan: without an index on the join column, the database engine has to read every row of that 12M row table to find matches. At 50K rows, a full scan takes milliseconds, the query returns, everyone moves on. At 12M rows, the same operation takes seconds to minutes, holds locks during that time, blocks other transactions trying to touch the same table, and can cascade into timeouts across unrelated parts of the system.

The subtle point for your conversation: the query optimizer may have been choosing the full scan deliberately at small scale because it was actually the right choice. For small tables, the overhead of an index lookup (follow the index structure, find the row pointers, fetch the actual rows) can exceed the cost of just scanning everything. The optimizer makes this calculation based on table statistics. At 50K rows, full scan wins. At 12M rows, the same calculation should produce a different result - but only if the index exists for the optimizer to consider.

For the immediate fix: add an index on the join column. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after to watch the query plan change from Seq Scan to Index Scan. That's the conversation with your colleague - not 'you wrote bad code' but 'the query plan that was optimal at development scale became catastrophic at production scale, and we need to give the optimizer better tools.'

EXPLAIN ANALYZE confirmed it - Seq Scan on the large table, cost estimates that are completely divorced from reality at this row count. the index fixed the immediate problem. but what I keep thinking about is the broader category. so much of software engineering is writing things that are correct, and correctness and performance are almost orthogonal concerns until suddenly they're not. a query can be semantically correct and operationally catastrophic. and this only shows up at scale. what's the systematic way to think about this class of problem so I can catch it earlier?

The systematic frame is: performance is a property of a system under a specific load, not a property of the code in isolation. This is why the correctness/performance split is so persistent and so dangerous. Correctness can be verified against a specification independent of scale - a unit test tells you the function returns the right value regardless of how many rows are in the database. Performance cannot be separated from context. The same query has different performance characteristics at 50K rows, 1M rows, and 12M rows, and those characteristics can differ by orders of magnitude.

The category of scale-revealed problems has a few recurring shapes worth knowing:

The complexity class surprise: your query was effectively O(n) with a small constant at development scale. At production scale n is 200x larger and the constant you couldn't see is now the whole problem. Full table scans are the classic version. Missing composite indexes on multi-column WHERE clauses are another.

The OFFSET pagination trap: SELECT * FROM table LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000000 makes the database generate and discard 10 million rows to give you 20. Works fine for page 1, catastrophic for page 500,000. Cursor-based pagination (WHERE id > last_seen_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20) is the fix - the database seeks directly to the cursor position.

N+1 queries: one query to fetch a list of N items, then one query per item to fetch related data. At N=10 this is unnoticeable. At N=10,000 this is 10,001 round trips. ORMs generate these invisibly and they're almost impossible to catch in development with small seed data.

The mitigation approach that actually works: realistic data volumes in a staging environment, slow query logging in production with alerting on anything above a threshold, and making EXPLAIN ANALYZE a standard part of code review for any query touching a table that will grow. The underlying discipline is treating queries as performance contracts, not just correctness specifications.
